newsitem.title: GERMANY: German opposition wants answers on Colombia agent.
newsitem.headline: German opposition wants answers on Colombia agent.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) on Tuesday demanded to know whether a German private detective arrested in Colombia was running secret missions for Bonn behind the back of the foreign ministry.

Werner Mauss, a shadowy figure who has worked for German police and intelligence in the past, was arrested last month on suspicion of paying a ransom to Colombian rebels to secure the freedom of the kidnapped wife of a German former executive.

Bonn has acknowledged that it "positively accompanied" what it calls Mauss's humanitarian mission, which has outraged Colombian authorities, and that Mauss met Chancellor Helmut Kohl's intelligence coordinator Bernd Schmidbauer.
SPD parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping said it was now time for Schmidbauer to show he was not running a "secret secret service" from the chancellery.

Scharping said he wanted to know if Schmidbauer arranged for Mauss to be supplied with German passports without the knowledge of the foreign ministry, and whether Mauss's involvement pushed up the ransom paid for the kidnap victim, Brigitte Schoene.
"If the answer to any of these questions is "yes', or even "half yes', the minister must resign," Scharping told reporters.

Speculation about Bonn's role in the affair has been stoked by the fact that Mauss carried a letter of support from the German embassy in Bogota when he was arrested, and had three passports, all genuine documents but issued with false names.

National ZDF television's Frontal magazine said that Schmidbauer, Mauss and two senior managers at chemicals firm BASF, the former employer of Schoene's husband, met in Bonn on November 12 to discuss payment of the ransom.
Schmidbauer has already been summoned to appear before parliament's foreign affairs committee on Wednesday.
Scharping said if the SPD was not satisified with his answers, it would consider calling a full parliamentary debate.

Colombian investigators accuse Mauss of being a member of the National Liberation Army (ELN) rebels and helping to support them with the ransom. Such payments are illegal in Colombia, which believes they provide an important source of income for the rebels.
Bonn, however, says it was involved in efforts to bring the Colombian government and rebels to the negotiating table.
The news weekly Der Spiegel said Schoene's abduction in August interfered with Schmidbauer's plans to help broker peace in Colombia.

Colombian Interior Minister Horacio Serpa, who met both Mauss and Schmidbauer in Bonn in July when he came to discuss the possibility of Germany hosting future peace talks, faces a motion of no confidence in the Colombian Congress over the affair.
